question: What are the factors hindering on-site deployments of construction robots?

answer.answer:
Hindering factors for taking robots onto live sites are organisational and environmental far more than mechanical: workforce training (RI6) is drawn on by 44 of the 50 coded cases, production/assembly restriction (RI19) by 25, delivery model and work culture (RI12) by 16, uncertainty in production (RI1) by 14 and regulatory and legal concern (RI18) by 12, and the first four of those carry little or no cited dependency structure, so the literature has largely not connected them to anything. The one requirement the cited literature puts directly upstream of on-site digital fabrication (PR8) is a mobile factory (CO12), a controlled enclosure rather than a machine, and it is drawn on by just 1 of the 50 while its onward step to robotic assembly (PR4) is carried by none of the 50: the structured-environment remedy is asserted and almost never exhibited. What is exhibited instead is mobility (AT9), drawn on by 28 cases, and off-site prefabrication (PR2) standing behind on-site assembly. Watch also that path-planning (PR12) is drawn on by 26 cases yet its cited link into robotic assembly is carried by only 2, so the planning layer and the assembly layer rarely appear together in the record.

**The site environment itself**

The cited literature gives on-site DFAB (PR8) one precondition: on-site DFAB has as a precondition a mobile factory, on the argument that environments need to be much more structured and controlled before construction robots can take over [1], backed by peer-reviewed evidence. That edge is carried by 1 of the 50 coded cases [2], and only 1 of the 50 draws on CO12 "Mobile factory" at all [2]. Its two onward edges are weaker still: CO12 enablesCapability PR4 "Robotic assembly" is carried by 0 of the 50 [2] and CO12 amplifies VA2 "Reduce time/improve productivity/efficiency" is carried by 0 of the 50 [2]. So the classic Japanese answer to the unstructured site, enclose it, is cited in the literature and carried by none of the 50 on the assembly path.

The route that is exhibited is the opposite one, bringing the machine to the site: AT9 "Mobile" enablesCapability PR8 "On-site DFAB" is carried by 9 of the 50 [2], against 9 of the 50 drawing on PR8 [2] and 28 drawing on AT9 [2].

**Regulation and safety**

PR8 dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", on standards evidence covering an alternative-means approval pathway for on-site printing, carried by 2 of the 50 [2]. 12 of the 50 draw on RI18, and it carries 5 cited edges in total, of which 2 are visible here [2], so no closed statement about its full dependency structure is available. The second visible one runs through collaboration: CO6 "Human-robot interaction" dependsOn RI18, on the grounds that collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards, carried by 2 of the 50 [2]. CO6 also mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern" via power-and-force-limiting operation, carried by 4 of the 50 [2]; 13 of the 50 draw on RI20 and it carries 3 cited edges in total, of which only this one is in front of me [2].

**Workforce**

This is the largest hindrance in the record. 44 of the 50 draw on RI6 "Require workforce training" [2], and it sits as a requirement under two central items: AR9 "Automated production workflow" dependsOn RI6, because sophisticated digital technologies prohibit adoption by less technologically familiar workers, carried by 38 of the 50 [2], and CO6 "Human-robot interaction" dependsOn RI6, since human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce, carried by 27 of the 50 [2]. 32 of the 50 draw on CO6 [2]. Alongside this, RE6 "Significant human involvement" is drawn on by 50 of the 50 and has no cited edge at all [2]: on-site robots in this record are not unmanned.

**Hindrances the literature has not connected**

25 of the 50 draw on RI19 "Production/assembly restriction", and it carries no dependency edges [2]. 14 of the 50 draw on RI1 "Increase uncertainty in production", also with no dependency edges [2]. These are among the most frequently coded obstacles and are invisible to any reasoning that walks edges only; the cited layer covers 68 of 140 enablers, which is a property of the literature rather than of the record [2]. The organisational variant does have one edge: PR4 dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", since robotics adoption rests on the environmental and organisational context, carried by 2 of the 50 [2], with 16 of the 50 drawing on RI12 [2].

**What on-site robotic assembly actually needs**

Of PR4's own cited requirements, RE2 "Robotic arm" is carried by 12 of the 50 [2], AT7 "Highly standardised" enabling PR4 is carried by 10 [2], PR12 "Path-planning" enabling PR4 by 2 [2], and PR4 hasPrecondition PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", on the grounds that automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials, by 4 [2]. Only one of these, the robotic arm, is a Resource; the rest are organisational or informational, which is the shape of the problem. 13 of the 50 draw on PR4 [2] and 26 on PR12 [2], so the gap between those counts and the 2 carrying the edge is itself the finding.

**In the deployed record**

The on-site cases bear out the maturity split. RP11 performs assembly, concrete work, rebar and steelwork on the structural core as a mobile robot on site and outdoors, at technology readiness level 7 [3], and RP18, doing steelwork and surface treatment on site, is also at technology readiness level 7 [4], as is RP22, which does 3d printing, assembly and material handling across sitework and the facade [5]. By contrast the handling and earthworks deployments are mature: RP12, digging and material handling on sitework, is at technology readiness level 9 [6] and RP14, heavy lift and material handling, likewise at level 9 [7]. Fabrication-type work on the open site is where readiness falls off.

Regulation appears explicitly as an adoption driver in one census record: census_RXT4-1 was adopted to address integration, market and regulation, performs assembly, material handling and timber joinery cutting on the structural core, at technology readiness level 9 [8], and the context attributes it to Firm_174 as developer. census_RXI5-1, adopted to address digital, safety and integration, performs digging, heavy lift and material handling on sitework at technology readiness level 8 [9], developed by Firm_081. The context carries these firms only as pseudonyms. The context does not link any of these cases to particular enablers, so I cannot say which hindrance enablers they exhibit.

One limit: the retrieved material does not cover location dependent/site constraint, machine error/immature technology, performance compromise/uncertainty, stakeholder scepticism or market access uncertainty, so this answer cannot speak to how often those are drawn on, and their absence here is not evidence about the record.

**Deployed evidence.** Selected by filtering the coded records, not by similarity. 13 records in the graph carry onsite as their deployment setting; all are listed below.
- RP1, adopted to address cost, labor, integration; performs 3d printing, concrete work; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP11, adopted to address digital; performs assembly, concrete work, rebar, steelwork; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP12, adopted to address labor, integration; performs digging, material handling; works on sitework; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP13, adopted to address digital; performs surveying & mapping; works on sitework; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP14, adopted to address cost, safety, labor; performs heavy lift, material handling; works on sitework; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP17, adopted to address digital, quality; performs inspection; works on the building envelope, the facade, or curtain wall; deployed on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP18, adopted to address quality, labor; performs steelwork, surface, surface treatment; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP19, adopted to address labor; performs concrete work, finishing, surface treatment; works on the structural core; deployed as a mobile robot, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
- RP20, adopted to address digital, labor; performs assembly, surface treatment; works on the interior fitout; deployed as a mobile robot, indoors, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP21, adopted to address digital; performs material handling; works on sitework; deployed off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP22, adopted to address cost, market; performs 3d printing, assembly, material handling; works on sitework, the building envelope, the facade, or curtain wall; deployed as a mobile robot, off-site, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 7.
- RP24, adopted to address digital; performs drilling; works on the interior fitout, services, mep; deployed as a mobile robot, indoors, on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 8.
- RP25, adopted to address labor; performs cleaning, material handling; deployed on site, outdoors; at technology readiness level 9.
